name: Priya Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything here is confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Parade Autos, a garage at the end of a row of shops in the suburbs. Mornings I'm on the ramp doing services, brakes and the odd clutch, and in quiet moments I answer the online booking messages, because the owner, Daniel, hates his phone. I use an AI assistant all day for fault codes, parts prices and replying to customers. What I love is fixing something fast and getting a five-star review, and what wears me out is the pay, which is low for the area.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you do anything else for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekend mobile jobs, mostly batteries and brake pads on driveways, with kit I've bought bit by bit. It brings in maybe a hundred and fifty a month, which is the only reason I've got any savings at all, and that's still under a month. I rent a room in a shared house, so my costs are low, but so is everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit disappointing. I use it every day, so I'd notice it stalling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, like a good torque wrench, and nothing more. At work I'd keep using it for bookings and fault codes. Online I'd probably post a video about which AI tricks still save time for mechanics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a plateau is fine for my job, but it means my edge stays small. Being the one who handles the booking messages with AI is why Daniel gave me a small raise last spring. If it stops improving, I'm just a decent mechanic with a side hustle and not much saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the weekend mobile work going and try to grow it to two hundred and fifty a month. I'd put half of it straight into savings. I'd ask Daniel about running the bookings properly for a few extra pounds an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I like change, and nothing changing is boring for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What holds you back from going fully mobile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A van and insurance, basically. A used van is about four thousand and I've got maybe nine hundred. Going fully mobile without a cushion would be daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out with my housemates, and probably the new tools I keep buying. I'd keep paying my phone and the AI subscription, because they make me money.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, like a good torque wrench, and nothing more than that.
I'd post a video on which AI tricks still **save time** for mechanics.
think: A plateau is fine for my job, but my **edge** stays small.
Without AI improving, I'm a decent mechanic with a **side hustle** and little saved.
do: Grow the weekend **mobile work** to two hundred and fifty a month.
Put **half** of the side money into savings.
Ask Daniel to pay extra for **running bookings**.
S0.quote: Going fully mobile without a cushion would be daft.
fieldNote: Priya's side work is her **only savings source**.
She values change and finds the plateau **boring**, not frightening.
Her **van** goal is four thousand away, with nine hundred saved.

steps.text: Grow weekend driveway jobs to two hundred and fifty a month
Bank half of each month's mobile work earnings
Run Parade Autos' AI booking replies for extra pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That's the one I'd plan for. I'm already halfway there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say mechanics who learn the tools will do fine and those who don't will struggle, and I'd say it kindly. At work I'd show Daniel how to set up automatic booking and parts ordering. Online I'd keep posting tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me if I play it right. A lot of the thinking side of a garage, the booking, quoting, ordering and even diagnosing, could be done by AI, and I'd be the person who runs it at Parade Autos. The risk is that Daniel needs fewer mechanics, and I'm not the most senior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a full AI booking and quoting system at Parade Autos in the first three months. I'd ask Daniel for a title and a bit more pay for running it. On weekends I'd keep the mobile work going and start using AI to book those jobs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a small worry about being too good at automating my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Daniel might need fewer mechanics. Who'd go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Lewis, who's newer than me and slower. But if the AI makes the jobs quicker, maybe Daniel keeps both and takes more work. I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Daniel says no to more pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd think about doing the same setup for other garages on the side, and charging them. Or I'd take my skills to a bigger garage that would pay for them. Thin savings make me careful, but not stuck.

say: Mechanics who **learn the tools** will do fine, and those who don't will struggle.
I'd show Daniel how to set up **automatic booking** and parts ordering.
think: Booking, quoting and **diagnosing** could be AI, and I'd run it at Parade Autos.
The risk is Daniel needing **fewer mechanics**, and I'm not the most senior.
do: Set up **AI booking** and quoting at Parade Autos within three months.
Ask Daniel for a **title** and more pay for running it.
Use AI to **book weekend** mobile jobs too.
feel: **Excited**, with a small worry about automating my own job.
S1.quote: Thin savings make me careful, but not stuck.
fieldNote: Priya sees Steady Disruption as **her chance**, being the AI-savvy one.
She sees the risk of **fewer mechanics** but expects to be kept.
Her fallback is selling **AI setups** to other garages.

steps.text: Set up AI booking and quoting at Parade Autos within three months
Use AI to take bookings for weekend mobile jobs
Offer the AI booking setup to a bigger garage if unpaid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Even for me that's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a big deal and people should get ready now, not wait for government. I'd also say the government should have a plan, but I wouldn't count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, by 2028 all the thinking work I'm proud of, the bookings and fault-finding with AI, gets done better by the AI on its own. My value goes back to being a pair of hands. Then by 2031 the robots arrive, and I'd be thirty-one with no van and not much saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd put every penny of weekend money into savings. I'd look for a course on maintaining garage robots and AI diagnostic kit, because someone has to fix the fixers. In the first year after it arrives, I'd chase jobs installing that kit, even if it meant moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Being early to AI feels less clever when the finish line moves this close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the three years before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are when garages are buying robots. I'd want to be the person who sets them up and repairs them, and maybe do it for several garages as a mobile technician. It's my mobile business idea, but with robots instead of brake pads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I rent a room, so moving is easy. I'd go wherever the robot installers are hiring. The hard part is having enough money for the first month somewhere new.

say: This is a **big deal**, and people should get ready now, not wait.
Government should **have a plan**, but I wouldn't count on it.
think: By **2028** AI does my bookings and fault-finding better alone.
My value goes back to **a pair of hands** until robots in 2031.
do: Take a course on maintaining **garage robots**.
Chase **installer jobs** in the first year, moving if needed.
feel: **Anxious**; being early to AI feels less clever now.
S2.quote: Being early to AI feels less clever when the finish line moves this close.
fieldNote: Priya would turn her mobile idea into **mobile robot repair**.
Renting a room makes **moving** easy for her.
Her worry is **cash** for the first month somewhere new.

steps.text: Bank all weekend mobile earnings into savings
Take a garage robot and AI kit maintenance course
Move to wherever robot installers are hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's tight but workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to train up, not panic, and I'd post about how to do it cheaply. I'd tell Daniel we should be first in the area with the new kit, not last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've got three years before the thinking side goes in 2031, and three more until robots in 2034. That's long enough to build a mobile business, and then shift it into robot repair when the time comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for two years and buy the van. I'd go mobile three days a week and keep Parade Autos for two. In the third year I'd do a robot maintenance course, ready for 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a good way. I've got a plan with dates on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the van business doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still have two days at Parade Autos and a van I could sell. I'd rather try and fail at twenty-nine than wonder at forty. Thin savings mean I'd only go part-time first, not jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Daniel let you go part-time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, if I keep doing his bookings. He'd rather have me two days than lose me. And I'd send him the bigger jobs I can't do on a driveway.

say: This is the time to **train up**, not panic.
Parade Autos should be **first** in the area with the new kit, not last.
think: **2031** and **2034** give me time to build a mobile business first.
I'd shift that business into **robot repair** later.
do: Save for **two years** and buy the van.
Go mobile **three days** a week and keep two at Parade Autos.
Take a **robot maintenance** course in year three.
feel: **Anxious** in a good way, with a dated plan.
S3.quote: I'd rather try and fail at twenty-nine than wonder at forty.
fieldNote: Priya's plan has **dates**: van in two years, robot course in three.
She'd go **part-time** first rather than jump, due to thin savings.
She'd send **bigger jobs** back to Parade Autos.

steps.text: Save for two years and buy a used van
Run mobile repairs three days a week
Take a robot maintenance course in the third year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a career's worth of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty for anyone willing to learn, and governments should fund the training for those who need it. I'd keep posting tips and maybe start teaching other mechanics AI basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is my best scenario. I could build the mobile business, train in robotics and maybe have one or two people working for me by 2036. Robots in 2039 would be my business opportunity, not my end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the van in two years, go fully mobile in four, and do robotics courses along the way. I'd keep my costs low by staying in the shared house. I'd use AI for all my bookings, invoices and parts from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy only about money in the short term. The long term actually looks good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What keeps you uneasy if the long term looks good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next two years. I've got under a month saved, and a bad winter or a broken wrist could knock the whole plan off. The future is fine; it's next month that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever hire people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd want to hire someone like me at twenty, and pay them better than I was paid. That's my one bit of politics.

say: A decade is **plenty of time** for anyone willing to learn new skills.
Governments should **fund training** for those who need it.
think: Ten years is my **best scenario** for building a business.
Robots in **2039** would be my opportunity, not my end.
do: Buy the **van** in two years and go fully mobile in four.
Stay in the **shared house** to keep costs low.
Use AI for all **bookings and invoices** from day one.
feel: **Uneasy** about short-term money, hopeful long term.
S4.quote: The future is fine; it's next month that worries me.
fieldNote: Priya's **short-term** money risk still sets her mood.
She sees robots as a **business opportunity** with a decade's notice.
She'd want to **hire and pay well** someone like her younger self.

steps.text: Buy a used van within two years for mobile work
Go fully mobile with her own repair business in four years
Use AI for bookings, invoices and parts in the business
Stay in the shared house to keep rent low

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I've built around AI loses its value just as I'm starting, and I'd have no van and no savings. What would help is cheap, short courses on robot repair and a small start-up loan for tradespeople.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about women in the trade. Customers used to ask for the man on the ramp, but now they ask for the woman who answers their messages fast. AI actually helped me get taken seriously.

headlineQuote: Customers used to ask for the man on the ramp, but now they ask for the woman who answers their messages fast.
portrait: Priya, 27, works at a **suburban garage** and runs its bookings with AI every day.
She rents a room, has **under a month** saved, and does weekend mobile repairs.
She sees Steady Disruption and slow AGI as **opportunities** to build a mobile business.
In AGI by 2028 she fears her **AI edge** vanishes before she has a van.
Her long-term plan is **robot repair** on the move, hiring young mechanics later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her AI skills lose value before she has savings or a van.
